street_smart.title: A traffic cop waves you down at a checkpoint during Bengaluru's current week-long drunk-driving crackdown. You had one drink at a work dinner a couple of hours ago and feel mostly fine. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Today's real report: Bengaluru traffic police booked 774 drunk-driving and speeding cases in a week-long enforcement drive (Deccan Herald). This scenario focuses on the moment a driver who's had 'just one drink' actually faces a checkpoint, since that's a far more common trap than driving visibly drunk.
street_smart.situation: The officer asks you to step out and take a breathalyzer test. There's a queue of vehicles behind you and you're already running late.

choices.text: Take the breathalyzer test calmly. If you're over the limit, accept the fine/process rather than arguing, and arrange a cab or a sober friend to take the vehicle home.
choices.feedback: Correct — 'feeling fine' isn't a legal defence, and cooperating keeps a checkpoint stop from turning into a bigger problem. If you're over the limit, the safest fix for tonight is leaving the vehicle and getting a cab, not trying to talk your way out.

choices.text: Quietly offer the officer some cash to 'settle it' on the spot instead of taking the test.
choices.feedback: This is the trap — during a publicised enforcement drive like this one, checkpoints are under extra scrutiny, and offering a bribe is a separate criminal offence on top of any drink-driving charge. It can turn a fine into an arrest for both the offer and the original stop.

choices.text: Chew gum or a strong mint right before the test and insist you 'barely had anything.'
choices.feedback: Breathalyzers measure alcohol in your breath directly and aren't fooled by mints or gum for more than a few seconds. Arguing your case at the checkpoint wastes time you could spend just cooperating and sorting out a ride home.

choices.text: Refuse the breathalyzer test outright since you don't think you're over the limit.
choices.feedback: Refusing a breath test is itself an offence under the Motor Vehicles Act and is usually treated the same as failing it. It doesn't protect you — it just adds a second violation to deal with.

takeaways: India's legal blood-alcohol limit is 30mg/100ml — for many people that's under one standard drink, so 'I feel fine' is not a reliable guide.
Refusing a breathalyzer test is its own offence under the Motor Vehicles Act — cooperating is safer than refusing.
Never offer cash to settle a traffic stop — bribing a public servant is a separate crime and escalates the situation, especially during a publicised crackdown.
